name: Iguta
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Only wordlists (Shimizu 1975, 1979; Gowers 1907) and a 2021 SIL sociolinguistic profile (Decker et al.) exist for Iguta; no grammar or phonology.

new_statements.quote: This kind of observation was useful in observing certain phenomenon such as tone marking in the words that were uttered by the participants because Iguta is a tonal language. During the interview session the participants were carefully observed by the researcher on how they pronounce each word from the data. [...] Tone plays a significant role in tonal languages. The change of tone affects the meaning of words in tonal languages.
new_statements.citation: Ado, Mohammed Ahmad & Siti Jamilah Bidin. 2017. Developing documentation of an endangered language: A case study of Iguta wordlist. European Academic Research 5(1): 871-908.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls in Iguta. The only first-hand prosodic statement is that Iguta is a tonal language (Ado & Bidin 2017, with a 455-item tone-marked wordlist of the Andirgiza dialect); Decker et al. 2021 (p. 12) add that no in-depth tone analysis has been done. Word stress/accent is not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone in citation-form wordlist items of the Andirgiza (Targwong) dialect, Jos North LGA; nothing about word- or phrase-level stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Iguta [nar], glottocode igut1238, East Kainji (Glottolog: Josa > Northern Josa; Ethnologue: Kainji, Eastern, Northern Jos, Jera). Ado & Bidin's data are from the Andirgiza (Targwong) dialect, treated as the standard; Decker et al. 2021 cover five clan lects (Andirigizah, Andigwong, Anabor, Anagohom, Andoho/Zangam) with 77-93% lexical similarity. Earlier scan verdict NO-SOURCE-FOUND is confirmed for stress; the scan missed the three open Ado papers (2017 x2, 2025), which are morphology/wordlist works and still silent on stress.

sources.quote: This kind of observation was useful in observing certain phenomenon such as tone marking in the words that were uttered by the participants because Iguta is a tonal language. During the interview session the participants were carefully observed by the researcher on how they pronounce each word from the data. [...] Tone plays a significant role in tonal languages. sources.note: p. 883: 'Iguta is a tonal language'; 455-item tone-marked wordlist of the Andirgiza (standard) dialect; no statement on stress or accent (grep = 0).

sources.citation: Ado, Mohammed Ahmed. 2025. A morphological study of infixes and infixation processes in the Iguta language. Al-Qalam: A Journal of Languages and Literary Studies 1(1): 134-142. doi:10.36349/alqajolls.2025.v01i01.015
sources.note: p. 135, second-hand and generic: 'Greenberg (1963) highlights that majority of African languages are genetically tonal, Hausa and Iguta inclusive'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Decker, Ken, Fittokka Gobak, Yakubu Danladi, Julius Dabet, Benard Abraham, Christina Riepe, Iris Sacson, John Sacson, Luther Hon & Adedamola Aregbesola. 2021. A Sociolinguistic Profile of the Iguta [nar] Language of Plateau State, Nigeria. Journal of Language Survey Reports 2021-019. SIL International. 69 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 6.3 (pp. 12-14) gives phone tables only; p. 12: 'there was no in-depth analysis of tones or other phonological features, nor has there been an effort to determine the phonemic status of phones.' Nothing on stress or accent anywhere; appendix wordlists (5 clans, 348 items) are tone-marked phonetic transcriptions.

sources.citation: Ado, Mohammed Ahmad & Siti Jamilah Bidin. 2017. Morphological description of noun formation process: Case of suffixation and prefixation in Iguta language. ASIAN TEFL 2(1): 17-40. doi:10.21462/asiantefl.v2i1.26
sources.note: Morphology only; 'stress' appears solely in the literature review (Matthews 1974 / Abubakar 2000 on Hausa). Tone-marked Iguta examples (rìshárí 'stone'); no Iguta stress statement.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger & Stuart McGill. 2012. The Kainji languages of Northwestern and Central Nigeria. Circulation draft, 369 pp. (cited as Blench 2014 by Decker et al.)
sources.note: Iguta mentioned only in the history of research (Gowers 1907 'Naraguta') and the East Kainji classification; per-language tone sections (Cinda, Hungwəryə etc.) do not include Iguta; East Kainji sec. 4.7 has no Iguta subsection. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2004. The status of the East Kainji languages of Central Nigeria: recent research. Draft for the Hamburg proceedings (Gerhardt retirement), 2 Oct 2004. 12 pp.
sources.note: Phonology and tone sections describe Boze only (four level tones); Iguta appears in the classification list and in the 'arm, hand' comparative appendix (iGuta ù-wiri / tì-ìri, tone-marked). No stress statement for any language.
